Only headlines and a few lines today, so this is a reaction, not a report.

Two headlines say the same thing from different angles: Trump has ordered federal contractors to check with the White House before responding to Congress. Nobody is stopping Congress from asking. The change is that the people holding the answers now need permission to give them.

It's a clever bit of plumbing, because oversight mostly runs through the people with the documents. A committee can subpoena a cabinet secretary, and that makes a good hearing. But the invoices, emails and project files sit with the contractors, and contractors have always been the easier door to knock on. They have no executive privilege to claim and they want future contracts. Put a White House checkpoint in front of that door and the quiet channel gets a lot louder and slower. Incoming House Intelligence chair Jim Himes has already said he wants to look at contractor donations to Trump's construction projects, so I doubt the timing is a coincidence.

The announced thing is a coordination policy. The implemented thing, if it holds, is a delay with a lawyer attached. And the new Congress doesn't take office until January 3, so the order lands in the gap, the same gap the Bloomberg headline hints at with "what Republicans can do before Democrats take control." Lame-duck periods are when everyone discovers which rules were really just habits.

Meanwhile Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion for air traffic control and blaming it for the airport mess, and the Iran war funding could shut things down again. So the branch being fenced off from the contractors is also the one being asked for the money. I'm curious who blinks first.
